To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the metabolism of l‐Dopa in Parkinson's disease is similar to that in normal subjects; (b) the major metabolite in urine is 3‐O‐methyldopa; and (c) 3‐O-methyldopa may act as an inhibitor of dopa decarboxylase in vivo.

the metabolism of orally administered DOPA in patients with Parkinson's disease is abnormal in that there is an increase in urinary excretion of the dopamine metabolite dihydroxyphenylethylglycol and a decrease in the excretion of the noradrenaline metabolite vanillylmandelic acid.

the urinary output of the dopamine metabolite homovanillic and dihydroxy phenyl acetic acid increased during l‐DOPAs treatment, but that the output of noradrenaline metabolite 4‐hydroxymandelic acid did not increase significantly, and that there was evidence of transamination of DOPA as a minor pathway.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the metabolic fate of orally administered L‐DOPA (3,4‐dihydroxyphenylalanine) in patients with Parkinson's disease.
the metabolism of orally administered DOPA in patients with Parkinsonism.
the metabolic effects of l‐Dopa in the treatment of Parkinsonism.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the therapeutic effect of l‐DopA in Parkinsonism is due to the conversion in the brain of this compound to dopamine, which is then metabolized by the normal pathways of dopamine metabolism.

the metabolic changes observed in patients treated with l‐DOPAs are in accord with the known metabolism of the drug in animals, but that some of the minor pathways are quantitatively more important in man.

the metabolism of DOPA in Parkinsonian patients differs from that in normal subjects in that it is characterized by a marked increase in the excretion of dopamine metabolites and by a minor but significant increase in the output of 4‐ hydroxy‐3‐ methoxyphenyllactic and m‐ hydroxyphenylacetyl acids.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the therapeutic action of DOPA in Parkinson's disease is due to its conversion into dopamine, which is then oxidized in a normal manner to homovanillic and dihydroxy‐phenylacetic acids.
l‐DOPAs action is mediated by a number of minor pathways of degradation.
the metabolism of orally administered DOPA is similar to that of endogenous dopamine, but with some additional metabolic routes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the metabolic fate of l‐Dopa in Parkinsonism is not significantly different from that in normal individuals.
l‐DOPa is a very powerful tool for studying the metabolism of l‐Dopa, but it is not a powerful tool for studying its effects on dopamine metabolism.
l‐DOPAs are not the only compounds that are used for the treatment of Parkinson's disease.
